title: Tokenizer throughput: prefill-side microsharding, caching, and ASCII fast-path
creator: Marco Liu
description:
Problem: Tokenizer and prompt preprocessing (the prefill-side work) is a significant CPU and latency hotspot for short requests. In production traces we see a non-trivial tail where requests spend 10-30ms in prefill tokenization + normalization before they see any decode work. This disproportionately affects small prompts, rate-limited workloads, and endpoints with aggressive latency SLOs.

Goal: Reduce end-to-end prefill latency and CPU-per-token by introducing a set of complementary optimizations: 1) microsharding and parallel tokenization for large batched requests and multi-input payloads, 2) a memory-backed prefix/tokenization cache with careful invalidation, and 3) an ASCII (fast) tokenization path + pre-tokenized request header reuse for common templates. Ensure changes are safe for the Dedicated/Private deployments (threading model and memory knobs), instrumented, and toggleable.

Success metrics: reduce median prefill latency by >=40% and p95 by >=30% for small prompts (<128 chars); reduce CPU cycles per token by >=20% for mixed workloads; increase cache hit rate to >=60% for templated prompts in beta customers.

Proposed approach (high-level):
- Fast path detection: implement a quick scan (byte-level, no Unicode normalization) to route ASCII-only inputs to a simplified tokenizer that avoids expensive Unicode codepoint handling and normalization steps. That fast-path should be the default for typical English prompts and micro-benchmarked for correctness.
- Microsharding: split tokenization work for multi-input requests and long prompts into micro-tasks scheduled across the prefill worker pool. Use job-stealing within the worker pool to avoid starvation and adapt shard sizes based on observed per-request token counts. Provide a per-request config to cap concurrency for Dedicated customers to control CPU isolation.
- Prefix / header reuse: detect common stored templates (e.g., system prompts, instructions) and keep pre-tokenized versions in an LRU cache keyed by normalized template id + model/vocab version. Return token id arrays directly on cache hits; hardware-agnostic.
- Cache design: in-memory LRU with configurable maximum memory size (MB) and TTL per-entry. Entries store token ids as compact arrays (uint16/uint32) to bound memory. Eviction policy: LRU with an optional frequency boost for recently used prefix templates. Provide per-tenant namespacing and a cache size override for Dedicated/Private deployments.
- Integration with prefill/decode scheduling: ensure tokenization micro-tasks yield to decode threads when decode backlog is high (avoid head-of-line blocking). Add backpressure signals from the decode queue to tokenization scheduler so tokenization can slow concurrency during decode overloads.
- Observability & safety: expose metrics (prefill.latency_ms.p50/p95, tokenizer.cpu_ns_per_token, tokenizer.cache_hit_rate, tokenizer.fastpath_rate, tokenizer.failed_fastpath_count). Add histograms for shard sizes and job scheduling latency. Provide toggles and dynamic flags for enabling fast-path/cache/microshard independently.

Constraints & trade-offs:
- Memory vs latency: larger cache yields better hit rates but increases memory footprint; Dedicated/Private installs may want stricter defaults.
- Correctness vs speed on fast-path: ASCII fast-path must be conservative about Unicode edge cases (emojis, combined characters) and fall back to the full tokenizer when ambiguity is detected.
- Complexity: microsharding increases scheduling complexity and potential contention; implement incrementally and keep a single-threaded fallback to simplify rollbacks.

Deliverables:
1) Design doc + correctness proofs for ASCII fast-path and cache keying (Confluence).
2) Prototype microshard scheduler and benchmark harness (worker-level unit/perf tests).
3) In-memory prefix cache implementation with eviction/TLS knobs.
4) Metrics dashboards and a canary rollout plan (hosted + dedicated).
5) Runtime flags and per-tenant configuration UI hooks in Console.

Rollout plan:
- Phase 1 (canary): enable ASCII fast-path + instrumentation for 5% of hosted traffic. Measure correctness and cache hit impact.
- Phase 2 (beta): add prefix cache behind flag for a small set of accounts and enable microsharding for multi-input endpoints.
- Phase 3 (gradual): enable for all hosted traffic and provide Dedicated customers with tuning knobs; ship tooling docs and Console controls.

Risks and mitigations:
- Incorrect tokenization for edge-case Unicode: add a fuzzing test harness using production prompt samples and multi-lingual QA. Roll back fast-path on mismatch rate >1e-4.
- Memory blowouts on large caches: default limits, per-tenant caps, and eviction telemetry alerts.
- Threading bugs in microshard scheduler: staged rollout with single-threaded fallback and heavy unit tests.
acceptance_criteria: p50 prefill latency for <128-char prompts reduced by >=40% in benchmark harness compared to baseline
tokenizer.cpu_ns_per_token reduced by >=20% on mixed workload synthetic test
tokenizer.cache_hit_rate >=60% for templated prompts in beta customers
no production correctness regression in canonical multilingual test-suite (0 mismatches) during canary
feature toggles for fast-path, cache, and microshard are available and documented
notes: Consider reusing existing token array compacting code from ENG-7241 to reduce memory overhead

2025-01-28 Rafael Gomez (reviewer): Reviewed cache keying approach; suggested including model vocab version and normalization salt to avoid cross-model contamination. Also recommended using a compact uint16 encoding for token ids where possible.
